title: I Let Payroll Deduct the Exact Minutes They Invented

parts.text: I opened my paycheck app and stared at a four-hundred-dollar deduction named ALIGNMENT. No explanation, just a smug little minus sign. I am twenty-three, first real office job, still learning to push back. I walked to HR with the printout still warm. Dana in payroll did not look up from her granola. "That's for the all-hands you missed." I said, "I was on the floor covering phones because Rhea told me to." Dana shrugged. "Rhea marked you absent. Policy is docking." Rhea manages with a smile and a calendar no one can edit. I found the Slack thread where she had written Priya stay on phones, skip all-hands. My name is Priya. I screenshot it. Dana said, "Then take it up with Rhea. I just run the numbers." I went to Rhea's glass office. She was eating a sad desk salad from a plastic clamshell. "You can't just appear in doorways," she said. I held up the deduction. "You told me to miss it." She stabbed a cherry tomato. "Culture is showing up. You didn't." I said, "You wrote stay on phones." She smiled. "That was a suggestion. Suggestions aren't protection." Behind her, the badge reader beeped as people returned from lunch. She emailed a spreadsheet cell that just said 400. My badge said I had been six minutes late once in March because the elevator stuck. I could see where this was going. I could also see the copy machine still jammed with her all-hands agenda.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The $400 is a fake round number, and she just posted that tardiness will be billed in whole hours.

social.video_title: They named a $400 deduction ALIGNMENT — Part 1/2
social.description: HR called it policy. My manager called the Slack order a suggestion. The spreadsheet cell just said 400. Would you have gone to payroll or to the fridge note?

parts.text: I billed them in whole hours. I arrived at 8:00:00 by standing in the lobby until the clock flipped, then badged in, then stood in the elevator another three minutes so I would not be early, because early had never been paid. I left at 5:00:00 exactly, even if a call was ringing. Rhea appeared at my cubicle. "This is childish." I pointed at the fridge. "Whole hours." She said, "Don't be literal." I forwarded Dana the Slack order, the $400 cell, and the fridge photo, plus my six-minute elevator incident from March. I asked, politely, for the written policy that turns six minutes into four hundred dollars. Dana's granola paused. Legal asked for a meeting that smelled like conference-room oranges. They reversed ALIGNMENT. They took the fridge note down. Rhea called it a misunderstanding in a team email that did not mention my name and still managed to be about me. I started job hunting on my lunch, which I now take in full because whole hours go both ways. Two weeks later the company posted an actual tardiness policy with minute math. It was fair enough that even Rhea had to badge like the rest of us. I framed a printout of the cell that said 400 and put it in my interview portfolio, which is unhinged, and it got me a better offer. She said thanks and offered me a granola bar. I took it. Alignment, apparently, tastes like honey oats.

social.video_title: I clocked whole hours until legal called — Part 2/2
social.description: The fridge note went both ways and the spreadsheet cell could not survive a written-policy question. I left with a better offer and a honey oat bar. Would you have framed the 400?
